title: The Effects of a Pre-Existing University Course About Sleep on Students’ Subjective Sleep Quality, Sleep Beliefs, and Pre-Sleep Arousal
content: Good sleep is essential for health, yet sleep is often overlooked due to academic, occupational, and social demands. This study investigates whether attending a pre-existing university course about sleep can improve students’ beliefs and attitudes about sleep, subjective sleep quality, and pre-sleep arousal. Methods: Seventy-five volunteer students (40 F, age = 21.5±3.78) completed the Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep (DBAS), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the Pre-Sleep Arousal Scale (PSAS) before attending a 3-month pre-existing course in Sleep Psychology (N = 50, 22 F, age = 21.5±2.40, S group) or in History of Psychology (N = 25, 18 F, age = 21.5±1.83, H group). At the end of each course, the same three questionnaires were administered. Results: Our results showed that, at the post-test, the S group improved sleep quality, reduced sleep disturbances, decreased cognitive pre-sleep arousal, and reduced dysfunctional beliefs and attitudes about sleep. Conclusions: These data suggest that attending a sleep course improves subjective sleep quality and pre-sleep arousal by reducing dysfunctional beliefs. These findings underscore the potential benefits of integrating sleep education into university curricula and reinforce the importance of addressing sleep as a key component of students’ health and well-being.
